# On Nakula: a letter to a colleague

*A letter to a colleague, 31 July 2026 — on the name Nakula, and on the forms that keep failing it.*

Your note said, roughly: surely the marks are a nicety. Permit me to use Nakula to show they are not.

First, the attestation. The attested form is **नकुल**, from the tradition's own record. The canonical transliteration is **Nakula**.

Say it aloud as the sources heard it: “nuh-KOO-luh” The marks are what carry that sound to a reader who has never heard it spoken.

On the plain form — and I want to be precise, because you pushed on this. The plain form *nakula* differs from the canonical *Nakula* only by convention of display — case, not content. It is *acceptable everywhere*: in legacy systems, in plain-text citation, in the DNS itself. What is not acceptable is what follows in the register: respellings that change the letters, not just their case.

One more thing, because it always surprises: the name did not stay home. Nakula is the Aśvins’ son in the epic’s divine-accounting, linking the heroic age to the Vedic physician-gods; and in later tradition the twins became the exemplars of brotherly symmetry — the epic’s only perfectly matched pair.  The veterinary and medical lore the epic assigns him passed into the practical traditions of horse-culture across the subcontinent.

And it never stopped working. The twins Nakula-Sahadeva are the subcontinent’s byword for matched pairs — in cards, in teams, in twins generally.  His name graced South Indian kings (Nakula of the Cōḻa line’s theophorics); and in the epic retellings, his quiet excellence is the standard against which the louder heroes’ fireworks are measured.

## The Convention's Own History

Long before IAST was formalized in 1912, Sanskrit had Pāṇini — the fourth-century-BCE grammarian whose rules describe the language's sounds with a precision no other ancient tradition matched. That heritage is why the convention is so exact: retroflexes (ṭ, ḍ, ṇ, ṣ) are not accented dentals but separate phonemes with separate meanings; long and short vowels (ā/a, ī/i, ū/u) change words, not just timing. IAST writes those distinctions down with underdots and macrons so that a reader who has never heard Sanskrit can still read it *correctly*. Dropping the marks is not transliteration at a lower resolution — it is a different, lesser claim.

## The Address, Without an Encoding Detour

The canonical form **Nakula** already uses ordinary Latin letters, so the address bar needs no special encoding narrative. The digital temple can preserve the spelling exactly as the scholarly record presents it. That is the practical point here: consistency between the source, the citation, and the public address.

This does not make every romanization equally valid. A wrong letter remains wrong even when it is easy to type. Canonical status still depends on the attested convention, never on convenience or registrar inventory.

Write back when you have checked the sources; they are better company than I am.

*— The Register*

## The Verdict

**Nakula** is the canonical form: attested, checkable, and enforced across the temple, the lexicon, the cards, the APIs, and this register. The plain form *nakula* shares that standing — the two are the same name in every system. The false forms above are documented so that no reader has to take the temple's word on faith — the violations are stated, the sources are named, and the register stands open to challenge on every line.

The temple of **Nakula** stands at [/nakula/](/nakula/).

The docket for this ruling: no false forms on the docket; no contested forms attested; the attestation rests on 4 cited sources — Mahābhārata, Ādi Parvan (the twins’ birth), Mahābhārata, Virāṭa Parvan (the incognito year), Mahābhārata, Bhīṣma & Droṇa Parvans (war record).
